report:
The evidence clearly shows that the answer is **yes** — denosumab (Prolia) does reduce the risk of vertebral fractures in osteoporosis. Your initial assumption of "no" appears to be incorrect.

**Key Evidence:**

The landmark **FREEDOM trial** (published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2009) was a 3-year, randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study of nearly 7,900 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. It demonstrated that denosumab, given subcutaneously twice yearly, reduced the relative risk of **vertebral fractures by 68%**, hip fractures by 40%, and nonvertebral fractures by 20% compared to placebo. This trial was the basis for the FDA's approval of Prolia in June 2010.

A **10-year open-label extension** of the FREEDOM trial (published in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology*, 2017) confirmed sustained fracture risk reduction, with yearly incidence of new vertebral fractures remaining low and similar to rates during the initial trial.

An **AAFP evidence review** concluded that denosumab is effective in reducing both vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

The **FDA-approved label** for Prolia explicitly states it "reduces the incidence of vertebral, non-vertebral and hip fractures."

**Important caveat:** If denosumab is discontinued, there is a significant risk of rebound vertebral fractures (including multiple fractures), so patients must transition to an alternative antiresorptive therapy.

**Sources:**

- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/
- https://www.aafp.org/afp/2019/0501/od1
- https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(17)30138-9/fulltext
